title: New Tablets and a Circumcised Heart
summary: Moses tells how God gave the Ten Commandments again on new stone tablets, which Moses placed in a wooden ark, and how God set apart the tribe of Levi to carry the ark and serve him. Then Moses asks what God requires of Israel: to fear him, walk in his ways, love and serve him, and keep his commands. The God who owns the heavens and shows no partiality loves the fatherless, the widow, and the foreigner, and Israel must circumcise their hearts and love the foreigner too.
story: Chapter 9 recalled the golden calf and Moses' long intercession, and it ended with Israel's future hanging on that prayer. Chapter 10 gives the answer: God renewed the covenant. The broken tablets were replaced, the words were written again, and the ark became their resting place. That act of mercy is the ground for the chapter's second half, one of the great summaries of what God asks of his people. It moves from law carved in stone to a heart that has been changed, a theme that will return in Deuteronomy 30 and in the prophets' hope of a new covenant written on the heart.
historical:
The renewal of the tablets is told in Exodus 34, and the making of the ark in Exodus 25 and 37. The ark was a wooden chest overlaid with gold, carried on poles, which later stood in the most holy place of the tabernacle and then in Solomon's temple. According to 1 Kings 8:9 it held only the two stone tablets. It disappears from the historical record, most likely lost or destroyed when the Babylonians burned the temple in 587 or 586 BC, and its fate has been the subject of many legends.

Verses 6 and 7 break into Moses' speech with a short travel record, set off in many translations as a parenthesis. It places Aaron's death at Moserah, while Numbers 20 and 33 place it on Mount Hor, and the order of the stopping places differs from Numbers 33:30-33 (see the hard question). The note about the Levites serving “to this day” (verse 8) presupposes a long-established priestly tribe. For the wider debate about the book's composition, see the note on Deuteronomy 5.
cultural:
In the ancient Near East, treaty documents were often stored in a sacred place, sometimes at the feet of a god's image, so that the gods could witness the agreement. Israel had no image of God, but the tablets of the covenant were laid in the ark, beneath the place where God was said to be enthroned between the cherubim. The ark was a kind of footstool for the invisible king, holding the terms of his covenant.

The chapter's concern for the fatherless, the widow, and the foreigner (verse 18) addresses the three most vulnerable groups in an ancient society built on family land and male heads of households. Without a father, husband, or place in a clan, a person had no one to plead their case and no share in the land. Ancient kings in Mesopotamia and Egypt boasted of protecting widows and orphans, as the epilogue to the laws of Hammurabi of Babylon does, but Deuteronomy goes further, saying God himself loves the foreigner and commanding every Israelite to do the same. Circumcision, the sign of the covenant cut into the body of every Israelite male since Abraham (Genesis 17), becomes in verse 16 a picture of what must happen inwardly.
literary: The chapter has two halves. Verses 1 to 11 finish the story of chapter 9, marked by the phrase “at that time” (verses 1 and 8) and by the return of the forty days and nights (verse 10). Verses 12 to 22 begin with “And now, O Israel,” a turn from story to appeal. The appeal is shaped by a pattern of description and command: God owns heaven and earth and chose Israel's fathers (verses 14 and 15), so circumcise your hearts (verse 16); God is “God of gods and Lord of lords” who loves the foreigner (verses 17 and 18), so love the foreigner (verse 19). The chapter ends with God's faithfulness in multiplying the seventy who went down to Egypt into a nation like the stars, which recalls his promise to Abraham in Genesis 15.

outline.t: New tablets placed in the ark
Aaron's death and the setting apart of Levi
God listens and sends the people on
What the LORD asks of Israel
The great God who loves the vulnerable: circumcise your hearts

doctrines.note: God is “the great, mighty, and awesome God, showing no partiality and accepting no bribe” (verse 17). His greatness is not only power but justice: he cannot be bought, and he defends those who have no one else to defend them.
The covenant broken at the golden calf is renewed at God's initiative. He writes the same words again, which shows that the covenant rests on his faithfulness more than on Israel's.

Holiness reaches the heart. Circumcision was the outward sign of belonging to God, but verse 16 calls for the inner reality it stood for: a heart open and yielded to God rather than stubborn and closed.

Israel's love for the foreigner is grounded in their own story, since they were foreigners in Egypt, and in God's own character, since he loves the foreigner. God's concern was never limited to one nation.

words.note: Mul, to circumcise. Here it is used figuratively: “Circumcise your hearts” (verse 16). The image pictures cutting away whatever covers and dulls the heart so that it can respond to God. Jeremiah repeats the call (Jeremiah 4:4), and Deuteronomy 30:6 promises that God himself will do it.

Ger, sojourner or foreigner, a person living among Israel without the land and family ties of a native. The ger had few rights and no inheritance. Deuteronomy commands care for the ger again and again, and this chapter grounds it in God's own love and in Israel's memory of Egypt.

Davaq, to cling or hold fast. It is the verb used when a man holds fast to his wife in Genesis 2:24. In verse 20 Israel is to hold fast to the LORD, a picture of loyalty that is close, personal, and permanent.

christ: The New Testament takes up this chapter's call for a circumcised heart. Paul writes that true circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit (Romans 2:29), and that believers were circumcised in Christ with a circumcision not done by hands (Colossians 2:11). What Moses commanded and what Deuteronomy 30 promised God would do, the New Testament sees God doing through Christ and the Spirit. The description of God as one who shows no partiality is echoed by Peter when he realizes that God welcomes Gentiles (Acts 10:34), and Jesus' care for widows, outsiders, and the poor shows the character of the God this chapter describes. The title “Lord of lords” is given to the Lamb in Revelation 17:14. These are connections the New Testament itself makes.

hard.q: Did Aaron die at Moserah or on Mount Hor?
hard.a:
Verse 6 says Aaron died at Moserah, but Numbers 20:22-29 and 33:38 say he died on Mount Hor, and Numbers 33:30-33 lists Moseroth before Bene-jaakan, the reverse of the order here. Readers have offered several explanations. Some suggest that Moserah was the name of a district or camp at the foot of Mount Hor, so both accounts describe the same event from different vantage points. Some note that Numbers 33 is a list of camps while Deuteronomy 10:6-7 is a brief note inserted for another purpose (to explain when the priesthood passed from Aaron to Eleazar), and that the Israelites may have passed through the same area more than once. Scholars who see the Pentateuch as drawn from several sources take the passages as preserving different traditions about the wilderness route.

The exact location of Mount Hor and of these camps is uncertain in any case. The purpose of the note is clear: even after the golden calf, God continued Aaron's priesthood through his son and set apart the Levites to serve him.

questions: Moses sums up what God asks: fear, walk, love, serve, and keep. Which of these comes most naturally to you, and which least?
What would it mean for you to have a circumcised heart, one no longer stubborn or covered over but open to God?
Israel was to love the foreigner because they had been foreigners. How might your own experiences of being an outsider shape the way you treat others?
